title: What time is it?
goal: Tell the time, name the days, and make appointments — while dodging one trap that catches English speakers every time: the Finnish "half" points to the NEXT hour.
bekal: name days with the ending **-na/-nä** and appointment times with **-lta/-ltä**
make, change, and cancel an appointment

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Sovitaan aika
dialogs.intro: Aino and Budi are looking for a time to study together before an exam.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Budi, meillä on koe ensi perjantaina. Opiskellaanko yhdessä?
lines.id: Budi, we have an exam next Friday. Shall we study together?
lines.literal: at-us is exam next on-Friday. study-shall-we-? together?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'd love to! When suits you?

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.id: How about Wednesday? At two, say.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hetkinen… Ei sovi. Minulla on työvuoro kahdesta kahdeksaan.
lines.id: Just a moment… No, that doesn't work. I have a work shift from two to eight.
lines.literal: moment… not suits. at-me is work-shift from-two to-eight.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.id: What about the morning? Half past ten?

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Juuri niin. Sama kuin indonesiaksi, eikö?
lines.id: Exactly. Same as in Indonesian, right?
lines.literal: just so. same as in-Indonesian, not-?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sama! Onneksi. Englanniksi se on aina väärin päin.
lines.id: Same! Luckily. In English it's always the wrong way round.
lines.literal: same! luckily. in-English it is always wrong way.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Sovitaan sitten keskiviikkona puoli yksitoista. Missä?
lines.id: Let's say Wednesday at half past ten, then. Where?
lines.literal: let's-agree then on-Wednesday half eleven. where?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: At the library? It opens at nine.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Sopii. Nähdään kirjaston edessä varttia vaille yksitoista.
lines.id: OK. See you in front of the library at quarter to eleven.
lines.literal: suits. let's-see library-'s in-front quarter-some short-of eleven.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Odota! Sanoit puoli yksitoista. Kumpi se on?
lines.id: Wait! You said half past ten. Which is it?
lines.literal: wait! said-you half eleven. which-of-two it is?

notes: **The big trap: puoli yksitoista = 10:30.** Finnish counts the half hour **toward** the next hour: *puoli yksitoista* is "half (on the way to) eleven". British English *half eleven* means 11:30 — exactly one hour later. Budi, as an Indonesian, is lucky: his language works like Finnish. For English speakers, this is the classic way to arrive an hour late. Train yourself: *puoli* + the **next** hour.

**Kahdesta kahdeksaan** — "from two to eight". Time spans use the pair of endings *-sta … -Vn*, exactly the endings you learned for places. Finnish treats time like a distance covered, and reusing these endings is one of the most economical things about the language.

**Kahdelta = at two (for appointments).** The ending *-lta/-ltä*, literally "from". Compare *kello kaksi*, which just names the hour. *Tulen kahdelta* = I'll come at two; *Kello on kaksi* = it's two o'clock now.

**Keskiviikkona** — days take the ending *-na/-nä*. *Maanantai → maanantaina*, *perjantai → perjantaina*. This is the essive ("as") ending, also used for dates and roles (*olen opettajana* = I work as a teacher, Unit 18).

**Sopiiko?** — "does it suit?". The verb *sopia* is used for anything that "fits": a schedule, clothes, a taste. Answer by repeating it: *Sopii.* / *Ei sovi.* Note the gradation in the negative: *sopii → ei sovi*.

**Sovitaan** — the "let's" form. Finnish has its own form for suggestions: *mennään!* (let's go), *opiskellaan* (let's study), *sovitaan* (let's agree). It looks like the impersonal form, and it is used far more often than *me menemme*.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: Finnish has two ways: the official one (24-hour, used in train timetables and the news) and the everyday one (12-hour, used in speech). The one you need to master is the second.
after: ⚠️ **Puoli always points to the NEXT hour.** *Puoli kolme* = 2:30, not 3:30. If you think in British English ("half three" = 3:30), you'll be exactly one hour off. Translate it in your head as "halfway to three".
*Yli* = past, *vaille* = to. The dividing line is minute 30: up to 30 you use *yli*, after 30 you use *vaille* with the next hour.
To ask: *Paljonko kello on?* or *Mitä kello on?* — both are equally common. To answer: *Kello on…* or just the number.

grammars.title: Days and appointment times
body: Two endings cover almost all scheduling: **-na/-nä** for days and dates, **-lta/-ltä** for clock times.
after: ⚠️ Numbers undergo gradation too: *yksi → yhdeltä*, *kaksi → kahdelta*, *viisi → viideltä*, *kuusi → kuudelta*. The first six numbers all change their stem; the rest are tamer.
*Keskiviikko* literally means "mid-week" — the only Finnish weekday name not borrowed from Scandinavian. Note that the Finnish week starts on **Monday**, so Wednesday really is in the middle.
**For half-hour times, the ending goes on the number**: *puoli kolmelta* (at half past two), *varttia vaille kolmelta*. In conversation people often just drop it: *Nähdään puoli kolme.*

blocks.text: *Ensi* (next) and *viime* (last) never change form, but the noun does: *ensi **viikolla***, *viime **vuonna***. Note that weeks take an "outer" ending (*-lla*) while months take an "inner" one (*-ssa*) — something you simply have to memorize.

blocks.title: Punctuality in Finland
items: Five minutes late already counts as late, and fifteen minutes late without warning is considered rude. Buses and trains leave on the minute, too.
If you're going to be late, let people know in advance — one short message, *Olen viisi minuuttia myöhässä, anteeksi*, solves the whole problem.

head: Suomi
English
rows: See you in front of the library.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Perua* (to cancel) is best used with a short reason: *Minun täytyy perua, olen kipeä* (I have to cancel, I'm sick). Canceling with no reason at all feels colder in Finland, even though nobody will tell you off.

The most common invitations use the "let's" form: *Mennään kahville!* (let's get coffee), *Nähdään huomenna!* (see you tomorrow), *Sovitaan myöhemmin* (let's sort it out later). You've already seen this form in the dialogue, and it is far more natural than building a full sentence with *me*.

exercises.prompt: Write the time in Finnish (the everyday way).
Change each day to the "on that day" form.
Change each hour to the appointment form (-lta/-ltä).

items: See you in front of the library.
